title: Why fingers wrinkle in the bath
hook: Wrinkly bath fingers are not soggy skin: your nerves actively make the wrinkles.
peek: Pruney fingers after a long bath are not just skin soaking up water. The wrinkles are made by the nervous system, which suggests they may have a job, though what that job is remains debated.
lede: Stay in the bath long enough and your fingertips pucker. For a long time people assumed the skin simply soaked up water and swelled. In fact the wrinkling is an active response. Researchers found in the 1930s that it depends on the nerves to the fingers, which tighten tiny vessels under the skin so the pads shrink and fold.

bullets.text: Because nerves control it, the wrinkling is something the body does, not something that happens to it. It appears mainly on the fingers and toes, and usually takes around five minutes in warm water.

In 2011 the scientist Mark Changizi suggested the wrinkles work like tyre treads, channelling water away so fingers and toes grip better in the wet. He noted that the patterns resemble river channels.
In 2013 a Newcastle University team asked people to move wet marbles between containers. Those with wrinkled fingers did it faster, while dry objects showed no difference.
A 2014 study elsewhere repeated a similar test and found no advantage from wrinkled fingers. So the wrinkles are certainly nerve-driven, but whether they really help us grip is still argued over.
